subject: literature
passage: The Hallett Cornet Band had eleven members, four of whom could read music, and it practiced on Thursday evenings in the back of Pruett's feed store, among the sacks of oats. Mr. Pruett, who led it, held no illusions about its quality. When the Ladies' Aid suggested that the band might rest until it improved, he only shook his head. In a town of forty houses on a treeless plain, he said, a man could go a whole week hearing nothing but wind and the complaints of his neighbors; yet on the Fourth of July, when the band marched down the single street playing more or less the same tune, people came out of every door. It was not the music they came out for, Mr. Pruett said, and the band need not be good to give it to them.
stem: Based on the text, why does Mr. Pruett want the band to keep playing?

choices.A: He expects the band to improve once more of its members have learned to read music.
choices.B: He believes the band draws the isolated town together, whatever the quality of its music.
choices.C: He wants to prove to the Ladies' Aid that the band plays better than they believe it does.
choices.D: He hopes the band's playing will drown out the complaints he hears from his neighbors.

explanation.why: Mr. Pruett admits the band is poor ("held no illusions about its quality"), but he notes that in a lonely town people "came out of every door" when it marched. He says "it was not the music they came out for" and that the band "need not be good to give it to them." He values the band for bringing the community together.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Mr. Pruett never predicts improvement; he argues the band need not be good.
explanation.B: Correct. His argument is that the band gives the isolated town an occasion to come together, regardless of skill.
explanation.C: Incorrect. He agrees the band is not good; he does not try to prove otherwise.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The neighbors' complaints describe the dullness of town life; he never says the band should drown them out.
